en: The Questions of King Milinda, Chapter on Duration: 1.
The Question on the Continuity of Phenomena (Dhammasantatipañha)
The King said:
"Venerable Nāgasena, is he who arises the very same person, or is it another?
The Elder replied:
“It is neither that same person nor another.
“Give me an analogy,” he said.
“What do you think, great king? When you were young, tender, delicate, and lying on your back, were you that very same person who is now grown up?”
“No indeed, venerable sir; that young, tender, dull-witted infant lying on its back was one person, and I, who am now grown, am another.
“If that were so, great king, then there would be no mother, nor a father, nor a teacher, nor one skilled in a craft, nor one possessed of virtue, nor one possessed of wisdom.”

“Great King, is the mother of the *kalala* one, the mother of the *abbuda* another, the mother of the *pesi* another, the mother of the *ghana* another, the mother of the small [embryo] another, and the mother of the large [embryo] another?
Is it one who learns a craft, and another who becomes skilled? Is it one who commits an evil deed, and another whose hands and feet are cut off?”
“Certainly not, venerable sir.
But when this is said, what would you say, venerable sir?
The Elder replied:
“Great King, I myself was once a young boy, tender and lying on my back; I myself am now grown up. It is by depending upon this very body that all those states are comprised as one.
“Give me a further simile.
“Great King, suppose a man were to light a lamp; would he keep it burning for the entire night?”
“Yes, venerable sir, it would burn all night.
“But, great king, is the flame in the first watch the same as the flame in the middle watch?
“No, venerable sir.”
“Is the flame in the middle watch the same as the flame in the last watch?
“No, venerable sir.
“Then, great king, was the lamp in the first watch one thing, the lamp in the middle watch another, and the lamp in the last watch yet another?”
“Certainly not, venerable sir; it was not by relying on that very same [wick] that it burned all night.
“In the same way, great king, the continuity of phenomena (dhammasantati) flows on: one arises and another ceases;
it flows on as if neither before nor after, yet it is neither that same thing nor something else. Thus, from the preceding consciousness to the succeeding consciousness...”
“It comes together,” [he said].
“Give me a further simile,” [the king replied].
“Just as, great king, when milk is being milked, after some time it turns into curd, and from curd into butter;”
“Suppose one were to exchange butter for curds. Now, Great King, if someone were to say:
‘That which is milk is the very same as curds; that which is curds is the very same as butter;
that which is butter is the very same as curds,’ would he, Great King, be speaking correctly?”
“Certainly not, venerable sir; it does not arise depending on that very same thing.
“In the same way, great king, the continuity of phenomena (dhamma-santati) flows on: one [moment] arises, another ceases;
it flows on as if neither before nor after, yet it is neither that same thing nor something else. Thus, from a preceding consciousness, a succeeding consciousness [arises].”
"It enters into inclusion.
"Well said, venerable Nāgasena!
This concludes the first question on the continuity of phenomena.
